title: Syllabus
text:
“Us and them” is one of the oldest structures in politics and one of the hardest to pin down. This seminar asks what happens to a democracy when that line hardens, and what group identity has to do with it.
We start with identity, where the concept comes from and how an attachment to a group becomes a political fact. Then we take the word “polarization” apart, because it names several different things and many arguments in this literature are really arguments about which one is meant. The middle of the term belongs to affective polarization, the tendency to dislike the other side rather than merely to disagree with it, and to the survey items that much of the evidence for it rests on. We end by pushing on the concept: what happens when the dividing line is religion or region rather than party, whether partisan animosity is about identity at all, and how much of the alleged damage to democracy holds up.

title: Syllabus
text:
Course objectives
The seminar is built around reading political science carefully rather than accumulating results. By the end of it you should be able to take a claim about polarization, work out what it is a claim about, and say what evidence would support or undermine it.
Three things run through every session. The first is conceptual discipline: polarization means several different things, and many disagreements in this literature are about which one is meant. The second is measurement: an affective polarization score is a construction, and what it is built from shapes what it can support. The third is evidence: a striking finding is a starting point rather than a conclusion, and the seminar asks what design produced it and how much it can carry.
The term paper is where you do this on a question of your own, with evidence you analyse yourself.

title: Syllabus
text:
Course logistics

General information
The seminar meets on Wednesdays, 15:30-17:00, in A5, 6 – C 112. Each session is built around the core reading, so the discussion only works if everyone has done it. Readings for each session are listed in Section 5 and the full references are collected in Section 6.






Tip



If you have to miss a session, tell me beforehand. A short email is enough, and it lets me tell you what you missed.




Prerequisites
Two different things go by this name, and it is worth keeping them apart.
Formally, the prerequisite depends on which of the two modules in Section 3.3 you register this seminar under. Whether you meet it is a question for the module catalogue and the Studienbüro, not for me.
In terms of what this course assumes, no prior work on polarization, party systems or political psychology is expected. The readings are research articles rather than textbook chapters, so you should be comfortable reading one, but learning how to read one is part of what the seminar is for.


Module and credits
This seminar is offered in both International Relations modules, and which one applies to you depends on how you register it. The credits, the assessment and the term paper word limit are the same either way. It counts toward either of:

Aufbaumodul: Internationale Beziehungen (Modulkatalog p. 31)
Schwerpunktmodul: Internationale Beziehungen (Modulkatalog p. 38)
Course type: Hauptseminar (HS)
Credits: 6 ECTS

The authoritative version of all of this is the module catalogue and the examination regulations for the B.A. Political Science, not this page. Where the two disagree, the regulations win.


What is required of you
Assessment has two parts, and the vocabulary is the examination regulations’ own. Coursework (Studienleistung) is assessed pass or fail, and passing it is a prerequisite for the graded work. The term paper (Prüfungsleistung) carries the mark.

Coursework, pass or fail
1. Active participation (Mitarbeit). Section 13b of the examination regulations allows participation to be set as coursework in a discussion-based course of this size, and it is set here. It is assessed on the whole of your contributions across the term, not on any single session. What counts is that you engage with the reading and with what other people say about it.
2. Doing the reading. Each session lists core reading, which everyone does, and optional reading, which is there for anyone who wants to go further and as a starting point for term papers. The core reading is mandatory rather than recommended. It is also the basis on which participation is assessed, because a discussion of a text nobody has read is not a discussion.
3. A term paper idea presentation (Referat). You pitch your term paper to the group in session 11 or 12. A few minutes on your question, why it is worth answering, and how you would answer it, followed by discussion. The point is to get criticism while there is still time to act on it.


Term paper, graded

Form: an empirical written term paper (schriftliche Hausarbeit), plus the code that reproduces its analysis.
Length: at most 7000 words, the limit set in the module catalogue.
Deadline: 15 January, 23:59.
Topic: your own, on something the seminar covers. You pitch it in session 11 or 12, and session 13 is optional individual consultation.

A workable paper takes a claim from the literature and confronts it with evidence you analyse yourself: it tests the claim against a case or a dataset it was not built on, re-analyses published data under a different measurement choice, or works out what two authors’ rival definitions do to the same data. A summary of what several authors have said is not a term paper, and neither is an argument that never meets data.






Important



Every paper produces results, and somebody else has to be able to recompute them. Hand in the script or the notebook that produced your numbers, tables and figures, together with the data or a link to where it comes from. Any technology is fine, R, Python, Stata or anything else, as long as the result comes out of a script that can be run again rather than out of clicks nobody can retrace.





Registration and withdrawal
Registration for the Prüfungsleistung, deregistration, and the applicable deadlines are handled by the Studienbüro under the examination regulations, not by me. Check the dates there and keep to them, because responsibility for meeting them sits with you.
If a good reason, illness in particular, prevents you from submitting the term paper on time, section 30 of the examination regulations applies. You must submit a written application to the Studienbüro without delay, with evidence. The examination board decides, and the burden of proof is on the applicant. Tell me as well, but telling me is not a substitute for the formal application.
Section 5 additionally allows deadlines for coursework and examinations to be extended on a timely written application, for instance for students with children or with dependants requiring care.


Disability and chronic illness
If a disability or a chronic illness makes it harder for you to take an assessment in the form it is set, you are entitled to compensation that restores equal opportunity, under section 6 of the examination regulations. Applications are made in writing and in good time, and applications on grounds of disability or chronic illness go to the university’s representative for students with disabilities or chronic illness.






Tip



Talk to me early, and tell me only what you want to. The formal route runs through the representative and the examination board, and I do not need to know the nature of your condition. What helps me is knowing early that an adjustment is coming, so it can be built in rather than improvised.




Language
The seminar is taught in English and the readings are in English. The term paper shall be written in English.


Additional learning resources
Two external platforms are worth your time. Both are voluntary and neither is part of the requirements to pass. They are here because the term paper asks for reproducible code, and this seminar spends its sessions on the reading rather than on tooling.
DataCamp. Use the link to join the course group, which gives you six months of premium access. DataCamp offers in-depth, self-paced practical training in R, coding, data analytics and AI topics, so it is the right place to drill something until it is automatic, at whatever speed suits you. The introduction to R track is a good starting point.






Warning



Register with your uni-mannheim.de address. Premium access is tied to the university account. If you sign up with a private address the group link will not grant it, and the fix is to start again with the right address.


Duolingo Math. Freemium, and a good starting point if you would like to relaunch yourself into mathematics fundamentals or introductory statistics. No prior statistics is assumed in this seminar, so this is not a prerequisite. It is simply there if the maths behind a reading feels shakier than you would like.


Mental health support
Life and study at the University of Mannheim can sometimes feel complicated, challenging, or overwhelming. That is completely normal.
If you ever feel mentally or emotionally strained, you may find useful advice on the university’s good mental health and studying page. The help in times of crisis page gives an overview of the counselling and support services available at the university.

AI policy






Note



This stated policy is a first proposal and may be subject to change during the term.


You may use AI assistance, and for some things it is genuinely useful: finding literature, checking whether an argument holds together, working on your English.
Two conditions.
Declare it. Your term paper carries a short note saying what you used and what you used it for. A sentence is enough. An undeclared use is a problem in a way that a declared one is not.
It does not make the argument. The claim, the reasoning and the judgement about what the evidence supports have to be yours, because they are what is being assessed. A paper that reads as though nobody decided anything is a weak paper whether or not a model wrote it, and you are answerable for every sentence you submit, including any citation that turns out not to exist.

title: Syllabus
text:
Session plan
What each session covers, what you should be able to do afterwards, and what to read. Dates are on the Schedule.






Note



This is a preliminary plan and may be revised during the term.



Session 1: Introduction and outlook

09 September 2026

What the seminar asks, how the term is organised, and what a term paper in it looks like. We also settle the schedule for the term paper pitches.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Describe what the seminar covers and how the three substantive blocks build on one another.
State what the term paper asks for, when the pitch happens, and what makes a question workable.


Optional

Torcal and Harteveld (2025)




Session 2: What is identity?

16 September 2026 · Concepts

Before we can ask what divides a democracy, we need a concept of the groups that do the dividing. This session treats identity as a demand for recognition and dignity, and asks how an attachment to a group becomes a political fact rather than a private one.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Trace where the modern concept of identity comes from and how it entered political argument.
Explain how a demand for recognition becomes a political demand.
Distinguish an identity from a preference, and say why the distinction matters for the rest of the term.


Core reading

Fukuyama (2018), chapters 1, 2 and 3

Optional

Huddy (2013)
Huddy (2001)
Westphal (2025)




Session 3: What is political polarization?

23 September 2026 · Concepts







Note



The core reading for this session was listed incorrectly at first. The intended readings are the 2008 exchange in the Journal of Politics between Abramowitz and Saunders (2008) and Fiorina et al. (2008). The Annual Review article by Fiorina and Abrams (2008), listed here before, is now optional. If you have already read it, your time was not wasted: it makes the same case as the reply, at greater length and with the concepts spelled out.


Polarization is a metaphor borrowed from the natural sciences, and political science has attached it to several different things: how far apart elites stand, how far apart voters stand, how tightly issue positions bundle together, and how far apart the camps feel. This session sorts them apart and asks which disputes in the literature are empirical and which are definitional.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Distinguish elite from mass polarization, and ideological divergence from issue alignment.
Explain why two authors can disagree about whether a public is polarized without disagreeing about any fact.
Identify which concept of polarization a given empirical claim depends on.


Core reading

Abramowitz and Saunders (2008)
Fiorina et al. (2008)

Optional

Fiorina and Abrams (2008)
Lelkes (2016)
Baldassarri and Gelman (2008)
McCoy and Somer (2018)
Turkenburg and Erkel (2025)




Session 4: What is affective polarization?

30 September 2026 · Concepts

Affective polarization (AP) is the tendency of people who identify with a party to view opposing partisans negatively and copartisans positively (Iyengar and Westwood 2015; Iyengar et al. 2019). This session takes the concept apart: the social identity logic it rests on, what it claims to add to an ideological account of division, and what evidence shows that partisan animus reaches beyond survey answers into implicit attitudes and behavior.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Derive in-group favouritism and out-group hostility from social identity theory.
Explain what affective polarization claims to add to an ideological account of division.
Assess the evidence that partisan animus shows up in implicit attitudes and behavior, and not only in what people say in surveys.


Core reading

Iyengar et al. (2012)
Iyengar and Westwood (2015)

Optional

Wagner (2024)
Iyengar et al. (2019)
Tajfel and Turner (1986)
Reiljan (2020)
Iyengar and Wagner (2025)




Session 5: Measuring affective polarization

07 October 2026 · Measurement

Almost everything we know about AP rests on one class of survey item: feeling thermometers and like/dislike ratings. This session asks what that item captures, how single ratings are aggregated into one score when there are more than two parties, and how those construction choices move the estimates and the conclusions that rest on them.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Say what a feeling thermometer measures and what it does not.
Reconstruct how an AP score is built in a multiparty system, and state what each step of the construction assumes.
Explain why the decision about who counts as a partisan changes the population an estimate refers to.
Judge whether a published estimate supports a comparison across countries or over time.


Core reading

Druckman and Levendusky (2019)
Wagner (2021)

Optional

Gidron et al. (2022)
Tyler and Iyengar (2024)
Tichelbaecker et al. (2023)
Kekkonen and Ylä-Anttila (2021)
Torcal and Comellas (2025)
Carlin and Love (2025)




Session 6: Beyond the thermometer: behavioral measures

14 October 2026 · Measurement

An attitude scale asks people what they feel. A behavioral measure asks them to do something: to divide money, to extend trust, to choose between candidates. We work through conjoint allocation games fielded across EU member states, and ask what a behavioral measure buys and what it costs.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Describe how a conjoint allocation game turns a choice into a measure of partisan animosity.
Compare behavioral and attitudinal measures on what each can and cannot support.
Explain why coalition partnership changes the pattern of animosity in European party systems.


Core reading

Hahm et al. (2024)
Stoetzer et al. (2023)

Optional

Westwood et al. (2018)
Carlin and Love (2013)
Wagner and Praprotnik (2024)
Röllicke (2025)




Session 7: Beyond party: social sorting and non-partisan identities

21 October 2026 · Extensions and consequences

Party is not the only line people sort along. This session asks what happens when party, region, religion, ethnicity and referendum camps line up with one another, and what happens when they cut across instead.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Define social sorting and explain why an aligned cleavage structure raises out-group animus.
Give a case in which the polarizing identity is not partisan at all, and say what makes it behave like one.
Assess how much support the evidence gives the claim that cross-cutting identities dampen animus.


Core reading

Harteveld (2021)
Hobolt et al. (2020)

Optional

Hahm et al. (2023)
Bradley and Chauchard (2022)
Balcells and Kuo (2023)
Bettarelli et al. (2023)
Roccas and Brewer (2002)
Mason (2016)
Zollinger (2024)
Mason and Versteegen (2025)
Hobolt and Tilley (2025)




Session 8: Is partisanship a social identity, or a cue about ideology?

04 November 2026 · Extensions and consequences

American work is split on what partisan animosity is actually about. One side reads it as group identity, dislike of them because they are them (party over policy). The other reads a party label as shorthand for policy positions, so what looks like identity is disagreement in disguise (policy over party). We follow the exchange and ask what evidence could settle it.
Afterwards you will be able to:

State the party-over-policy and the policy-over-party positions and the evidence each rests on.
Explain why identity and categorisation are hard to separate in survey and experimental designs.
Specify what evidence would distinguish the two accounts, and why it is hard to obtain.


Core reading

Orr et al. (2023)
Dias and Lelkes (2022)

Optional

Orr and Huber (2020)
Dafoe et al. (2018)
Huddy et al. (2015)
Klar et al. (2018)
Bankert and Stone (2025)




Session 9: Consequences of affective polarization for democracy

11 November 2026 · Extensions and consequences

AP is usually introduced as a danger, to democratic norms, to accountability, to the willingness to live alongside people who vote differently. Recent work is more careful. Some of the alleged consequences do not survive better designs, and others hold only under particular conditions. This session separates what is established from what is asserted.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Reconstruct the argument for why AP is supposed to harm democracy.
Name the consequences that have actually been studied, and the designs used to study them.
Distinguish findings that hold up from findings that depend on context or on measurement.


Core reading

Harteveld et al. (2026)
Broockman et al. (2023)

Optional

Voelkel et al. (2023)
Versteegen et al. (2026)
Kekkonen and Harteveld (2025)
Somer and McCoy (2025)




Session 10: Open session

18 November 2026 · Extensions and consequences

This slot is deliberately unallocated. We settle the topic and the reading in the session before, so it can follow whatever the group most wants to pursue, whether that is a theme from earlier in the term or something none of the readings covered. Bring suggestions.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Propose a topic or a reading, and say what the seminar gains from it.
Read a text without a prepared framing, and take part in a discussion the group has shaped itself.



Session 11: Term paper pitches I

25 November 2026 · Term papers

Short pitches of your term paper plan, followed by discussion. Half the group presents and the other half asks the questions.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Present a research question, why it is worth answering, and a design that could answer it, in a few minutes.
Name the data or the texts your paper will work from.
Give another student criticism they can still act on.



Session 12: Term paper pitches II

02 December 2026 · Term papers

The second half of the pitches, in the same format.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Present a research question, why it is worth answering, and a design that could answer it, in a few minutes.
Name the data or the texts your paper will work from.
Give another student criticism they can still act on.



Session 13: Term paper consultation (optional)

09 December 2026 · Term papers

Optional individual consultation on the term paper. There is no group session in this slot. Email me to book a time.
Afterwards you will be able to:

Leave with a question, an outline and a plan you can execute before the deadline.

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Session 04 goals


read the goals aloud
goal 1 is the first half of the session, goals 2 and 3 the two papers


By the end of today, you will be able to:

Derive in-group favouritism and out-group hostility from social identity theory.
Explain what affective polarization claims to add to an ideological account of division.
Assess the evidence that partisan animus shows up in implicit attitudes and behavior, and not only in what people say in surveys.

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Today


0 to 5 min: goals and agenda
bridge from last week: from where people stand to how they feel



Why groups?

An evolutionary reading

Categories in the head

Why we see borders where there are none

Social identity theory

Ingroup favouritism and outgroup derogation

Iyengar, Sood and Lelkes (2012)

“Affect, not ideology”

Iyengar and Westwood (2015)

“Fear and loathing across party lines”

Wrap-up

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Group membership


we are group animals
belonging was a matter of survival, not preference
Baumeister and Leary: people form bonds readily and resist losing them, across cultures
Dunbar: primate group size tracks neocortex size, humans sit at the top end
ingroup vs outgroup: who shares food, who is a threat
TODO: one concrete example to open with



Belonging is a fundamental human need, not a taste (Baumeister and Leary 1995)
Our large brains co-evolved with living in large groups (Dunbar 1993)
A group means an ingroup (share, cooperate) and an outgroup (compete, beware)

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
An old species


H. sapiens recognisable in Africa by about 315k years ago (Jebel Irhoud)
the old “behaviourally modern since ~50 to 70k” story is contested: McBrearty and Brooks find modern behaviours building up gradually in the African Middle Stone Age
so do not put a hard 70k number on the board
foragers today: mean band about 28 adults, mostly unrelated (32 societies)
settled mass societies are a very recent add-on
point: a mind tuned to bands now lives in mass democracies
TODO: timeline figure?



Homo sapiens is roughly 300,000 years old (Hublin et al. 2017)
Modern behaviour built up gradually, with no sudden “revolution” (McBrearty and Brooks 2000)
For almost all of that time: small, mobile bands of a few dozen adults (Hill et al. 2011)
The same minds now live in democracies of millions

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Invented borders


Tajfel and Wilkes: eight lines of different length
labelled A (short four) and B (long four): people exaggerate the gap between A and B
and see lines within A, within B, as more alike
no labels, or random labels: no distortion
the category does the work, not the stimulus


Once we sort a continuum into categories, we

overestimate differences between categories
underestimate differences within them


Label lines “A” and “B”, and people see the gap between A and B as larger (Tajfel and Wilkes 1963)

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
The colour example


light is a continuous spectrum of wavelengths
colour names are cuts we make in it, languages cut differently
ask: where exactly does blue end?



The spectrum is continuous
The colour names, and the borders between them, are ours



Figure 1: The visible spectrum, roughly 400 to 700 nm. The light changes continuously, and every border between named colours is drawn by us. Source: Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
From categories to bias


transfer to people: once “us” and “them” exist, the same distortion applies
Quattrone and Jones: Princeton vs Rutgers students, rival school seen as more alike
them: all alike, very different from us
us: all individuals
leads into SIT: categorisation is its first step



The same distortion, applied to people
Them: all alike, and very unlike us
Us: a collection of individuals (Quattrone and Jones 1980)

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Tajfel and Turner


social identity: the part of the self-concept that comes from group membership
categorisation: sort people, self included
identification: take the group on as part of who I am
comparison: judge us against them
positive distinctiveness: we want our group to look good next to others


Social identity is the part of the self that comes from group membership (Tajfel and Turner 1986)

Categorisation: sort people, yourself included
Identification: the group becomes part of who you are
Comparison: judge us against them


We seek positive distinctiveness: our group should look better

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Minimal groups


Klee vs Kandinsky, or dot estimation
schoolboys, groups with no history, no interaction, no stakes, anonymous
still: allocate more to own group, even give up absolute gain to maximise the gap
Billig and Tajfel: works even when assignment is openly random
point: the category alone is enough



Assign people to groups on a trivial basis: Klee vs Kandinsky, dot estimates
No history, no contact, no self-interest at stake
People still favour their own group, and even trade gains to widen the gap (Tajfel 1970; Tajfel et al. 1971)
It works even when assignment is openly random (Billig and Tajfel 1973)

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Two kinds of bias


ingroup favouritism: liking and helping us
outgroup derogation: disliking and hurting them
Brewer: not the same thing, ingroup love does not require outgroup hate
Balliet et al., meta-analysis of cooperation games: d = 0.32, and the gap is mostly ingroup favouritism
hold this: Iyengar and Westwood find the opposite for party
ask: which of the two is more dangerous for democracy?



Ingroup favouritism: liking and helping us
Outgroup derogation: disliking and hurting them
Distinct, and the first does not require the second (Brewer 1999)



In cooperation experiments, discrimination is mostly ingroup love (Balliet et al. 2014)
Keep this in mind for Iyengar and Westwood

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Party as identity


bridge to the readings
if party is a group like any other, SIT predicts affect, not only disagreement
that is the claim of affective polarization
the definition: Iyengar and Westwood, restated in the Annual Review
two parts, not one: ingroup favouritism and outgroup animosity, back to the last slide
“people identifying as partisans”: somebody has to decide who counts



If a party is a group like any other, partisans are an us
Then SIT predicts affect, not only disagreement: warmth for our side, hostility for theirs


“the tendency of people identifying as [partisans] to view opposing partisans negatively and copartisans positively” (Iyengar and Westwood 2015, 691; Iyengar et al. 2019)

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Introduction


links to last week: the Abramowitz vs Fiorina debate is about ideology
their move: look at affect instead
social distance: Bogardus, how close would you let a member of group X come?



Last week’s debate asked whether policy views have moved apart
ISL: that is the wrong test
Look at how partisans feel about each other, as social distance (Bogardus 1947)

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Theory


SIT applied to parties: identity implies ingroup warmth and outgroup hostility
salience: the more salient the identity, the more biased
campaigns: louder, longer, more negative since the 1970s
partisan cable news confirms stereotypes



Party identification is a social identity
Identity implies warmth for us and coldness toward them
Campaigns make the identity salient, and negative ads feed the dislike

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Research design


six surveys, 1960 to 2010
ANES thermometers 0 to 100, 1978 to 2008
traits: intelligent, selfish, closed-minded …
marriage: “how would you feel if your son or daughter married a …?”
UK as a stringent baseline: class-rooted parties, should be more polarized
two explanations tested: policy attitudes, campaign exposure (battleground states, 2004 attack ads, 2008 panel)



Thermometers: how warm do you feel toward each party? (ANES, 1978 to 2008)
Social distance: traits of party supporters, a child marrying across party lines
Comparison: United States vs United Kingdom, 1960 vs 2008 and 2010
Explanations: policy attitudes, exposure to campaigns

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Results: thermometers


in-party flat, around 70
out-party down about 15 points since 1988, just above 30 in 2008
compare: Protestants rate Catholics 66, Republicans rate “people on welfare” 50
same flat pattern for liberals and conservatives: party, not ideology








Figure 2: Mean feeling thermometer ratings of the own and the other party among Republicans and Democrats, ANES 1978 to 2008. In-party ratings stay near 70, out-party ratings fall toward 30. Source: Iyengar et al. (2012), Figure 1.




It is the out-party that has changed

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Results: social distance


1960: 4 to 5% of US partisans displeased by an out-party marriage
2008: 20 to 27%, 2010: 33 to 49%
UK: modest rise, now below the US
reversal: in 1960 the British cared more
policy attitudes predict affect only modestly, cultural issues not at all
campaigns: battleground residents polarize faster in 2008, small effect of attack ads








Figure 3: Share of partisans upset, displeased or unhappy if their child married a supporter of the other party, United States (top) and United Kingdom (bottom), 1960, 2008 and 2010. The US share rises from about 5% to between a third and a half. Source: Iyengar et al. (2012), Figure 4.




Policy views explain little of this, campaigns a little

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Conclusion


affect, not ideology: dislike grows even where issue positions barely move
partisanship is an affective attachment, acquired early and stable
worry: losers who despise the winners may not accept their decisions as legitimate
ask: is this a US story? the UK comparison says partly
ask: if partisans barely disagree more but dislike each other more, what is the “polarization” in affective polarization?



Affect, not ideology: Americans dislike the other side more, without disagreeing much more
Partisanship is an affective bond more than a set of views
Risk: opponents’ decisions may stop counting as legitimate

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Introduction


survey answers could be cheap talk, or filtered
question: does animus show up where people cannot or do not control it?
and in choices outside politics?



ISL showed what partisans say
Survey answers can be filtered or exaggerated
Does animus show up where people cannot hide it, and in nonpolitical choices?

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Theory


race as the benchmark: the deepest divide in American society
norms suppress open racial bias
no norm suppresses partisan bias, elites model hostility
H1: partisan affect implicit, H2: partisan bias at least as large as racial
H3: partisans discriminate in nonpolitical choices, H4: more out-group hostility than in-group favour



Benchmark: race, the deepest American divide
Social norms restrain racial bias, no norm restrains partisan bias
Expect partisan bias to be automatic, as large as racial bias, and driven by dislike of the out-party

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Research design


all online SSI samples, 2012 and 2013
Study 1: brief implicit association test (BIAT), party and race, N about 2,000
Study 2: pick one of two high-school seniors for a scholarship, cue is Young Democrats / Young Republicans or a racially typical name, GPA varied, N about 1,000
Study 3: trust and dictator games, player 2’s party and race crossed, N about 800
Study 4: add a no-party control and an independent, to separate favour from hostility, N about 1,250
figure shows: one BIAT screen (top) and the eight party images (bottom)

the respondent sorts images and words as fast as possible
here one key means “Democrats or Good”, the other key everything else
four rounds of 20: two pair Democrats with good, two pair Republicans with good

figure means: people answer faster for pairs they already link in memory

a Democrat who likes Democrats is quick when “Democrat” and “good” share a key
D-score = speed difference between the two pairings, divided by its SD, range -2 to 2
positive = faster with Republicans + good, negative = faster with Democrats + good
the race BIAT is identical, with Black and white faces or names






Implicit: reaction-time test of party and race associations
Scholarship: choose between two students, one cue for party or race, grades varied
Games: split $10 with a copartisan or opponent, same or other race
Games with a control: separate favour for us from hostility to them








Figure 4: The partisan brief implicit association test. Respondents sort party images and good or bad words with two keys, as fast as they can. Source: Iyengar and Westwood (2015), Figure 1.

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Results: does the test work?


figure shows: mean partisan D-score (dot) with 95% confidence interval (bar)

top: by party identity, strong Republican to strong Democrat
bottom: by ideology, very conservative to very liberal
right of zero = implicit preference for Republicans, left = for Democrats

figure means: the implicit test lines up with what people report

strong Republicans .35, weak Republicans in between, independents near zero
weak Democrats -.26, strong Democrats -.21: a small kink at the Democratic end
very conservative .23, conservative .17, liberal -.28, very liberal -.27
this is the validity check: the test measures party affect, not noise
D-score and thermometer gap correlate at r = .42









Figure 5: Mean partisan D-score with 95% confidence intervals, by strength of party identity (top) and by ideology (bottom). The implicit preference follows self-reported party and ideology. Source: Iyengar and Westwood (2015), Figure 2.




The implicit measure sorts people the way their self-reports do

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Results: saying vs reacting


figure shows: distributions of affective polarization among Democrats (dark) and Republicans (light)

top: explicit, net feeling thermometer, from -100 to 100
bottom: implicit, partisan D-score, from -2 to 2
the smaller the overlap of the two curves, the more polarized

figure means: both measures separate the parties clearly

effect size (Cohen’s d): 1.72 explicit, .95 implicit
so partisans look more polarized when they state their feelings than when they react automatically
the opposite of race, where people hide bias in surveys
the two measures share only 17.5% of their variance

ask: why would people exaggerate partisan dislike when asked?








Figure 6: Distributions of explicit (top, net feeling thermometer) and implicit (bottom, partisan D-score) partisan affect for Democrats and Republicans. The two parties overlap little on both, and least on the explicit measure. Source: Iyengar and Westwood (2015), Figure 3.




Explicit answers are more polarized than automatic reactions

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Results: party vs race


figure shows: mean D-score with 95% CI

top: partisan BIAT by party, bottom: race BIAT by race
same metric for both tests, so the gaps can be compared directly

figure means: party divides more deeply than race, even implicitly

Republicans .27, Democrats -.23, independents -.02
whites .16, African Americans -.09
effect size: party d = .95, race d = .61
partisan and racial D-scores correlate only .13: party is not a proxy for race
race is acquired at birth and deeply ingrained, so this is a high bar









Figure 7: Implicit association scores for party (top) and race (bottom), means with 95% confidence intervals. Democrats and Republicans lie further apart than African and European Americans. Source: Iyengar and Westwood (2015), Figure 4.




The party gap is larger than the race gap, even implicitly

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Results: leaners


figure shows: mean net feeling thermometer (Republicans minus Democrats) with 95% CI

five groups: Democrats, leaners, pure independents, leaners, Republicans

figure means: leaners feel like partisans

Democrats -48.8, lean Democrats -30.6
independents +3.5, close to neutral
lean Republicans +28.2, Republicans +42.6
leaners are less polarized than partisans, but far from independents
“closet partisans”: saying “independent” is a label, not an absence of affect

ask: who counts as a partisan? back to the definition




Figure 8: Mean net feeling thermometer, Republicans minus Democrats, with 95% confidence intervals, by party identity including leaners and pure independents. Leaners sit close to the partisans, pure independents near zero. Source: Iyengar and Westwood (2015), Figure 5.

Leaners behave like partisans, only pure independents are neutral

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Results: scholarship


table shows: share of participants picking each scholarship winner, N in parentheses

top: partisan task, rows are the participant’s party
bottom: racial task, rows are the participant’s race
pooled over all four GPA conditions

table means: party drives the choice, race barely does

Democrats pick the Democrat 79.2%, Republicans the Republican 80.0%
leaners too: 80.4% and 69.2%
independents slightly pro-Democrat, 57.9%
race: only African Americans favour their own, 73.1%
whites pick the Black student 55.8% of the time
the party cue was one line among five activities on a CV









Figure 9: Winner of the scholarship by the participant’s party (top) and race (bottom). About 80% of partisans pick the candidate of their own party, while race produces far weaker ingroup choice. Source: Iyengar and Westwood (2015), Table 3.




Four in five partisans pick their own side

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Results: merit


figures show: predicted probability, from a logit model, with 95% CI

top: probability of picking the Republican, by participant’s party
bottom: probability of picking the African American, by participant’s race
three panels each: equally qualified, one or the other has the better GPA (4.0 vs 3.5)

figures mean (party): grades do not matter

a Democrat picks the Republican .21 when equal, .30 when the Republican is better, .14 when the Democrat is better
Republicans pick the Democrat at most about .2 in every panel
no interaction between party and qualification is significant
independents roughly split, slight lean to the Democrat

figures mean (race): grades do matter

whites pick the white student .42 when equal, .29 when he is worse, .64 when he is better
African Americans pick the Black student about .78 when equal, and pick the white student .45 when he is better

ask: what would it take for merit to beat party?








Figure 10: Predicted probability of picking the Republican, by participant’s party (top), and of picking the African American, by participant’s race (bottom), for equally qualified candidates and for each candidate being more qualified. Partisan choices barely respond to grades, racial choices do. Source: Iyengar and Westwood (2015), Figures 6 and 7.









Party trumps merit, race does not

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Results: games


games: player 1 gets $10 and may give any part to player 2

dictator game: player 2 just keeps it, so giving less is pure dislike
trust game: the gift is tripled and player 2 may send some back, so giving is also a bet on trustworthiness

figure shows: mean amount given (dot) with 95% CI

player 2 is a copartisan or an opposing partisan (rows)
of the same or a different race (panels)
dictator game on top, trust game below

figure means: party moves money, race does not

overall means: $2.88 dictator, $4.17 trust
copartisans get about 24% more in the dictator game, about 10% more in the trust game
same race: +8 cents in dictator, -7 cents in trust, neither significant
no interaction: a copartisan of the same race gets no extra









Figure 11: Mean amount of $10 given to player 2 in dictator (top) and trust (bottom) games, by player 2’s party and race, with 95% confidence intervals. Copartisans receive more than opponents in both games, while race makes no difference. Source: Iyengar and Westwood (2015), Figure 8.




With real money at stake, party matters and race does not

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Results: by party


table shows: mean allocation to player 2 and its standard error, and the share giving nothing

rows: participant’s party x player 2’s party
dictator game on top, trust game below

table means: both sides discriminate, by about the same amount

dictator: Democrats give Democrats $3.82, Republicans $3.14
Republicans give Republicans $3.36, Democrats $2.68
the copartisan premium is $0.68 for both parties
trust: premium $0.63 for Democrats, $0.24 for Republicans
Republicans give less overall
one in three Republicans gives a Democrat nothing in the dictator game









Figure 12: Mean amount given to player 2, with standard errors and the share giving nothing, by the participant’s and player 2’s party, in the dictator and trust games. Both parties give more to their own side. Source: Iyengar and Westwood (2015), Table 4.




The bias is symmetric: each side gives its own about 68 cents more in the dictator game

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Results: love or hate?


figure shows: mean amount given to player 2 with 95% CI, Study 4

player 2 is an opposing partisan, an independent, a copartisan, or undescribed (control)
the control is the baseline: no party information at all

figure means: hostility is at least as strong as favouritism

dictator: copartisan +$0.67, opponent -$0.63 against the control
trust: copartisan +$0.30, opponent -$0.63
in the trust game the penalty is about twice the bonus
independents are treated like the control
contrast with Balliet et al.: in most groups discrimination is ingroup love, for party it is outgroup hate

ask: is a party the same kind of group as a minimal group? why hostility here, where most groups produce favouritism?








Figure 13: Amount of $10 given to player 2 in dictator and trust games, by player 2’s party, means with 95% confidence intervals. Opponents receive less than the no-information control, copartisans more. Source: Iyengar and Westwood (2015), Figure 9.




In the trust game the penalty for opponents is about twice the bonus for copartisans

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Conclusion


ask: is a scholarship choice or a money split better evidence than a thermometer rating? what can each miss?
partisans, unlike racists, face no sanction
party is chosen, so people are blamed for it
elites who cooperate look like appeasers, so taunting pays
limitation: in the studies party is revealed, in real life it must be discerned



The party divide is as deep as race, or deeper, and it reaches nonpolitical choices
It is permitted: no norm restrains it
Hostility toward them outweighs favour for us
Elites have an incentive to fight rather than cooperate

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Recap: takeaways


ask for one takeaway before revealing the list



Groups are old, and categories distort how we see people
Social identity theory: a category alone is enough for bias
Affective polarization: dislike of the other side, measured apart from policy views
In the US it has grown since the 1980s, while in-party warmth stayed flat
It shows up implicitly and in behaviour, and exceeds racial bias

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:
Recap: learning goals


goal by goal
ask for each answer before revealing it


Goal 1. Favouritism and hostility from social identity theory

Categorisation, identification, comparison, and the wish for positive distinctiveness
Favouritism and derogation are distinct. Party seems to trigger both.

Goal 2. What affect adds to ideology

Division can grow in feelings while policy views stay put
ISL: out-party ratings fall, policy attitudes explain little

Goal 3. Animus beyond survey answers

Implicit tests and costly choices show the same bias, with no norm to restrain it

title: Session 04: What is affective polarization?
text:

Today we asked whether it exists. Next we ask how well our measures capture it.

title: Us and them: Identity and polarization in contemporary democracies
text:
What this course is
“Us and them” is one of the oldest structures in politics and one of the hardest to pin down. This seminar asks what happens to a democracy when that line hardens, and what group identity has to do with it.
We start with identity, where the concept comes from and how an attachment to a group becomes a political fact. Then we take the word “polarization” apart, because it names several different things and many arguments in this literature are really arguments about which one is meant. The middle of the term belongs to affective polarization, the tendency to dislike the other side rather than merely to disagree with it, and to the survey items that much of the evidence for it rests on. We end by pushing on the concept: what happens when the dividing line is religion or region rather than party, whether partisan animosity is about identity at all, and how much of the alleged damage to democracy holds up.
The last three sessions belong to your term paper: two of short pitches to the group, and one of optional individual consultation.

A is the respondent’s party and also their most-liked one, so all three measures can be computed
ask before going on: is this person polarized? how much?

title: Session 05: Measuring affective polarization
text:
Reiljan: the affective polarization index


Equation 3: the AP of party n’s partisans: own party minus each out-party, weighted by out-party size
the 1 minus V_n renormalises, so the out-party weights sum to 1
Equation 4: the system index weighs each partisan group by its own size
Reiljan uses partisan group means (the like/dislike matrix), so this is a party-system index
applied to one respondent: unweighted 10 minus 14/3 = 5.33, weighted 4.25
implicit choices:

in-group = declared closeness to a party, leaners included
only partisans get a score, non-partisans are dropped by design
one in-group only, B at 9 counts as an out-party

Reiljan says so himself: “API leaves out a substantial part of the electorate” (p. 381)










Figure 3: Distances from the respondent’s own party, Party A, to each other party, unsquared. Source: adapted from Reiljan (2020).



Unweighted: \(10 - \frac{9+4+1}{3} = 10 - 4.67 = \mathbf{5.33}\)


\[
AP_n = \sum_{m \neq n} (\text{Like}_n - \text{Like}_m) \frac{V_m}{1 - V_n}
\tag{3}\]
\[
API = \sum_{n} AP_n \times V_n
\tag{4}\]
\(n\) is the in-party, \(m\) an out-party, \(V\) a vote share.


In-group: the party you feel close to
Only partisans get a score
One in-group: B counts as an out-party









Note


How to read it. For the supporters of each party, take how much more they like their own party than each rival, and let bigger rivals count more. Then average these party scores, letting bigger parties count more.

title: Session 05: Measuring affective polarization
text:
Wagner: mean distance


same anchor as API, now defined as the most-liked party rather than the declared one
n_p is the number of parties without the most-liked one
the only change on the figure: the distances are squared, 1, 36, 81
D alone contributes 81 of 118
6.27 vs 5.33 from the same ratings: squaring weighs the most disliked party most
weighted 5.45 (weights renormalised over the three other parties, which is what Wagner’s Table 1 implies)
implicit choices:

in-group = top rating, chosen from the outcome itself
anyone who rates 2+ parties gets a score, partisan or not
still one in-group











Figure 4: The same distances from the most-liked party, now squared. Source: adapted from Wagner (2021).



Unweighted: \(\sqrt{\frac{1+36+81}{3}} = \sqrt{39.3} = \mathbf{6.27}\)


\[
\text{Distance}_i = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{p} (\text{like}_{ip} - \text{like}_{\max,i})^2}{n_p}}
\tag{5}\]
\[
\text{Distance}^{w}_i = \sqrt{\sum_{p} v_p (\text{like}_{ip} - \text{like}_{\max,i})^2}
\tag{6}\]
\(n_p\) counts the parties other than the most-liked one, \(v_p\) is a vote share.


In-group: the party you rate highest
Anyone with two ratings gets a score
Squaring stresses the most disliked party









Note


How to read it. How far each other party falls below your favourite, on average, where large gaps count extra because they are squared. The weighted version lets bigger parties count more.

title: Session 05: Measuring affective polarization
text:
Wagner: spread of scores


no anchor party at all: deviations from the respondent’s own mean, here 6
squared deviations 16, 9, 4, 25, sum 54, divided by 4 parties
divide by n_p as Wagner does, which reproduces his Table 1
(the version dividing by n minus 1 gives 4.24, that is the standard deviation used by Ward and Tavits)
weighted: the mean itself is vote weighted, 7.45, and the spread is 3.37
implicit choices:

no in-group needed
everyone with two ratings, including non-partisans
allows blocs: liking A and B, disliking C and D is fully polarized

Wagner’s preferred measure is the weighted spread










Figure 5: Squared deviations of each rating from the respondent’s own mean rating, 6. No party serves as the anchor. Source: adapted from Wagner (2021).



Unweighted: \(\sqrt{\frac{16+9+4+25}{4}} = \sqrt{13.5} = \mathbf{3.67}\)


\[
\text{Spread}_i = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{p} (\text{like}_{ip} - \overline{\text{like}}_i)^2}{n_p}}
\tag{7}\]
\[
\text{Spread}^{w}_i = \sqrt{\sum_{p} v_p (\text{like}_{ip} - \overline{\text{like}}_i)^2}, \quad \overline{\text{like}}_i = \sum_{p} v_p \, \text{like}_{ip}
\tag{8}\]


No in-group at all
Everyone with two ratings gets a score
Allows blocs: two liked parties against two disliked ones









Note


How to read it. How far your ratings scatter around your own average rating, with no party treated as yours. The weighted version lets bigger parties count more, both in the average and in the scatter.

title: Session 05: Measuring affective polarization
text:
Why weight?


the like/dislike battery lists every party side by side, as if they were equal
they are not: Wagner’s example, disliking the AfD matters less for German politics than disliking the CDU
and if the AfD doubles its vote, the same dislike should count for more
practical reason: surveys differ in how many small parties they list, weights damp that
cost 1: three more choices (which election, which vote shares, renormalise or not)
cost 2: AP moves when vote shares move, even if nobody’s feelings changed
Reiljan’s Greece: Syriza went from 5 to 27%, so its weight in the index rose more than fivefold between 2009 and 2012
ask: is that a bug or a feature?


The scale shows every party as an equal line, but parties are not equal in size.

For: disliking a 40% party says more about a system than disliking a 3% one (Wagner 2021)
For: surveys list different numbers of small parties, and weights damp that
Against: more choices to make and report
Against: AP changes when vote shares change, even if no feeling changes (Reiljan 2020)







Note


Weighting answers a different question. Unweighted: how polarized is this person’s view of all parties? Weighted: how polarized is this person’s view of the parties that matter for the system?

title: Session 05: Measuring affective polarization
section: Does the choice matter in practice?
text:
Does the choice matter in practice?


figure shows: country means of AP in CSES, 51 countries, four measures
black = spread, grey = mean distance, circles unweighted, squares weighted
figure means:

levels differ a lot between measures: distance is always higher than spread
but the country ranking barely changes: correlations around .9

the US sits mid-table, not at the top
associations with turnout, satisfaction with democracy hold across measures, with some differences

so: the choice matters for levels, less for rankings, but you only know that because he computed all four

Rankings barely move: the measures correlate at about .9

The US is average in this comparison

title: Session 05: Measuring affective polarization
text:
Population of inference


each in-group rule defines who gets a score
and who gets a score defines whose AP the mean describes
API: partisans (with leaners), Distance and Spread: anyone with 2+ ratings
Druckman and Levendusky also restrict to partisans and leaners
“partisans in Germany are polarized” vs “Germans are polarized” are different claims
ask: which population does your research question need?


Do we want the AP of

partisans (attached to a party)?
voters (voted for one)?
partisans and voters?
the whole sample?
The answer fixes how the in-group is coded
And it fixes whose AP the estimate describes
API: partisans only. Distance and spread: anyone who rates two parties.

text:
Say whose AP


the same measure in two countries can describe very different shares of the public
so a cross-national difference can be a difference in who was counted
holds over time too: partisanship declines, the partisan pool changes








Important


Be clear whose AP you study. Your in-group rule decides who gets a score, and so which population your estimate describes. In a comparison across countries or over time, report the sample composition next to the estimate.




A partisans-only estimate in Latvia describes about a third of respondents, in Denmark about four in five
A difference between them may be a difference in who was counted

text:
Back to the definition


the definition from last week
it is about people: copartisans and opposing partisans
now look at what the item asks: how warm do you feel toward the Republican Party
ISL themselves conceded: “We will not be able to clarify whether respondents were thinking of partisan voters or party leaders”
thermometers of partisans exist too: D&L rate “party voters”, the 1980 ANES asked about “Democrats” and “Republicans” (D&L, footnote 3)
the standard item, and nearly all comparative data, targets the party



“the tendency of people identifying as [partisans] to view opposing partisans negatively and copartisans positively” (Iyengar and Westwood 2015, 691)


The definition is about people: fellow citizens who support a party
The standard thermometer asks about parties

title: Session 05: Measuring affective polarization
text:
Vertical and horizontal


Areal and Harteveld name the distinction
vertical: upward, toward parties, leaders, elites
horizontal: sideways, toward ordinary citizens who support another party
the definition is horizontal, the standard item is vertical
horizontal is what social division means: would I hire one, date one, trust one
the two need not move together



Vertical AP: affect toward parties and their elites
Horizontal AP: affect toward ordinary citizens who support them (Areal and Harteveld 2024)
The definition is horizontal
A party thermometer is vertical, a thermometer of party voters is horizontal
They are related, but not the same thing







Important


Be clear which AP dimension your measure captures. A party thermometer speaks to feelings about parties and elites. A claim about citizens disliking each other needs a measure that targets citizens.

Recap: takeaways

In two-party systems, AP is the in-party minus the out-party rating, averaged over any group
In multiparty systems, API, distance and spread give different numbers from the same ratings

goal by goal
ask for each answer before revealing it


Goal 1. What a thermometer measures

Warmth toward parties, which respondents read as their elites, not toward fellow partisans

Only with the same measure, and with the sample composition reported

text:
Each section is an argument (1)


intro: puzzle, or importance, or both, then a sneak preview of every other section
theory: why, given the literature and your own reasoning, things should be the way you expect
design: why this data, this measure, this analysis can answer the question

Introduction: why your research question is interesting (puzzling), or important, or both. Then a short overview of all other sections.
Theory: why, based on the literature and your own reasoning, things should be the way you expect. Ideally: why your hypotheses follow logically from the state of research.
Research design: why your data, measurement and analysis are well suited to the question and the hypotheses. Be open about what the data can and cannot do. Do not overclaim.

the grading scheme will follow later, it assesses all five parts


Empirical analysis: why the patterns in your results support, or contradict, your hypotheses and interpretations. Again, be honest about what the method can and cannot say.
Conclusion: a recap of the whole chain of argument, and why your study contributes to the literature.
